newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan sees progress in Afghan mediation effort.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan sees progress in Afghan mediation effort.

text.p: A Pakistani emissary held talks with Afghanistan's Taleban Islamic movement on Tuesday and called them a "step forward" in Islamabad's efforts to organise peace talks between warring factions.
Senior Foreign Ministry official Iftikhar Murshed met Taleban officials in the southern Afghan town of Kandahar for about four hours, Pakistani officials said.
In an interview with the state television later, he called the talks very useful and said: "I have no hesitation in saying that it was definitely a step forward."
He said he would now carry ideas to the opposition alliance based in the northern town of Mazar-i-Sharif, but gave no date for the visit.

Murshed last met Afghan opposition leader General Abdul Malik in Mazar-i-Sharif on July 1 after talks with Taleban officials in Kandahar and later said he had found the two sides too far apart to make peace.

The opposition alliance had proposed demilitarisation of the Taleban-held capital Kabul and formation of a political commission to consider the establishment of a broad-based government in the war-shattered country.
Taleban agrees to the formation of a political commission but has rejected the idea of the demilitarisation of Kabul, which it captured last September.

Taleban also wants a ceasefire and the release of hundreds of its fighters and several senior officials held as prisoners in Mazar-i-Sharif as a precondition for peace talks, which Pakistan has proposed should also be attended by Afghanistan's immediate neighbours as well as the United States and Russia.
The official APP news agency quoted Murshed as saying on Monday that Pakistan would not impose any formula on Afghans.
"We wish that the Afghan people themselves find out some formula for permanent peace," he said.
Pakistan recognised the Taleban government in late May after the purist Islamic militia briefly captured Mazar-i-Sharif with Malik's help. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates did the same.
Islamabad is accused by ethnic Uzbek and Tajik opposition factions of helping the mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban, which controls more than two-thirds of Afghanistan.

The Taleban captives include some key leaders who had gone to Mazar-i-Sharif for talks with Malik, who made a short-lived alliance with the Taleban against former opposition warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
Malik turned on the Taleban at the end of May, linking up with a Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat faction to drive them from Mazar-i-Sharif after 15 hours of street fighting.
